dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Two cuttings hang on the trade basket. One looked pale out in the sun. One looked dark under the roof. The dyer wants to know whether they match. The ferry crew wants to know whether they can fold the cloth away. Both have written “ready” on their slip.

options.text: Clip the two slips and take the same two cuttings on one board.
Leave the two cuttings on their hooks.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Sefa has clipped a small book note to the board. Ibn al-Haytham used experiments to check claims about light. The dyer points to the shade below the west tree and the clear stone farther along the lane. Carry both cuttings at once. The same board will fit on either stand.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Here the tree shades the whole stand. Bring the board under it. Keep the same side of each cutting facing you.

options.text: Slide both cuttings under the shade on their board.
Keep the board in hand.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Both cuttings look dark blue-grey in the shade. A thread at each corner still picks up the light. Neither stands out as the paler one on this board.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The clear stand takes the same board. Both cuttings can face the open light without moving their clips.

options.text: Put the same board in the open light.
Keep the board in hand.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Both cuttings look paler here. The difference seen when the cuttings were on separate hooks does not return. These two look alike when they share the light. The folds are still a separate question.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The dyer can now compare the cuttings in the same light. At the box, the ferry hand presses a corner of the full cloth. “I call it ready when it can go into the basket without damp folding against damp.” Both checks need to travel with the cloth. Put one at the front and hang the other alongside.

options.text: Hang the shared-light comparison at the front of the dyer’s line.
Hang the crew’s folding check by the basket with the comparison beside it.
Leave both tags loose while I think.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The dyer pins the same-light note at eye level. A customer brings two cloth corners for the dyer to compare on the same stand. Lower down the ferry note still asks if the folds are dry enough to pack.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The ferry hand turns the basket tag to “check folds first.” A crew member checks the cloth before packing it. A second slip beside it tells the dyer to compare both cuttings in the same light.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: A guild stub names Order 34, the box of blue lantern caps. “Due before the second square bell.” The clerk filed the stub with the other orders he approved before the first bell. Someone has chalked “boat late” on the margin.

options.text: Clip the guild stub with its due-bell line.
Leave the stub in the tray.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Orrin taps a small copy from the Nexus. Loud’s grant date shows when the patent office acted. “Same with my stamp. I can vouch for the time on the permit. The desk didn’t see the box reach the landing.” A crooked notch shows where the paper was split.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The landing basket has a strip for Order 34. Beside the line with the blue lantern caps sit two bell-shaped marks. A porter takes one bell tally when she gives up a load. The person who receives it adds another.

options.text: Clip the ferry strip with the two handover marks.
Leave the strip on the basket.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The crew reads a pair of marks as both sides of a handover. The guild uses its bells to mark hours of work. The ferry strip has no arrival time. It has the same crooked notch as the other half of the order.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: A reader has slid the ferry’s two bell shapes under the guild’s second-bell deadline. The box of caps waits beside the reader’s tray. Turn the stub and strip until their torn edges meet. Keep the deadline and the handover marks on separate lines.

options.text: Line up the two Order 34 notches and leave a space for the arrival time.
Leave the split copy on the board.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The notches match. One note tells when the order was due and when someone approved it. The other tells whose hands the box passed through. The landing time still has no mark. The reader wipes the chalked “late” away and leaves the question.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The buyer wants something she can bring back to the guild. The ferry crew want the marks they use to stay on the strip. You can put both pieces together under an order heading or keep the crew’s strip and hang a key with it.

options.text: Set both records under one order with separate headings for time and handover.
Keep the ferry marks with their key and leave an arrival slip for the next order.
Leave the proof with the buyer while I think.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The buyer folds the pair with Order 34 on top. She shows the guild the margin and the handover marks. The arrival line stays open when the box goes to the lantern bench.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The ferry crew tack the guide beside their basket. A later order will get its own arrival slip. The clerk leaves Order 34 open where the arrival time would go, while the buyer moves the box to the lantern bench.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Hana has sent a runner from the washhouse. The step is wet and no water is reaching the rinse tray. Somebody blamed the closed intake. The caretaker has opened her sight cover. From here, you can see water pass the head peg.

options.text: Clip the head-peg reading and follow the channel for this round.
Leave the reading with the caretaker.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Leave the intake as it is for this round. See what reaches the tray below the lane and look behind the catch screen farther west. A dry tray alone cannot tell you where the flow stopped.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: At the far side of the washhouse the rinse tray is dry below the tail peg. A thin run goes beside it and across the low step. The tray only catches what comes through its own branch.

options.text: Clip the tail-peg reading and mark the run beside the tray.
Leave the tail marker for now.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The caretaker keeps both marks in the same round. One records what entered the channel. The other shows what reached this tray. Water on the step cannot fill that space in the record.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Water has collected at the place where the channel narrows. A mat of leaves sits at the catch screen. Some water goes around the screen and joins the run across the step. The tray sits beyond the leaf mat.

options.text: Follow the little side run and clip where it leaves the channel.
Leave the screen where it is.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The three notes point to the screen as the place to try a clearing. A repair still needs a check downstream. Keep a separate question about whether people can get across the step.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Hana has one helper until the end of the shift. The washers need water in the tray. The carriers need a dry walk past it. Have the helper try the screen first, or put out the side crossing and leave the screen to the next crew.

options.text: Clear the leaves at the screen and leave the catch screen in place.
Open the side crossing and leave the screen for the next crew.
Keep the order on the hook for now.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The helper clips a note to the screen and clears the leaf mat. The intake stays at the mark you read. Go from the head peg to the tray again before telling the washers what changed.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The helper sets out the dry side step and points carriers around the run. The screen stays in place. Check the head peg again, then find what has changed at the crossing and the tray.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: You come back to the head peg. Water still passes the same notch. Clip this reading beside the one from before the helper started.

options.text: Keep the second head-peg reading with the first.
Leave the clip at the head peg.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The two readings have the same starting mark. Now compare what reaches the tray and where the carriers can walk.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: At the same head peg water still passes. Now it also reaches the rinse tray. The run across the step is thinner in this round. There is space on the screen note for the next crew’s reading.

options.text: Mark flow restored this round and leave the next check open.
Keep the reading in hand.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The side step is dry where the carriers walk. Water still runs across the low step and the rinse tray is dry below its peg. The route around the water worked. The tray needs its own repair.

options.text: Mark the crossing open and keep the tray repair on the board.
Keep the reading in hand.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: A washer uses the tray again. The caretaker hangs the source and tail readings together for the next crew. A carrier can see the narrower run and still chooses where to put her feet.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Two carriers take the dry side step. The washer moves her pail to a different tray for now. The two jobs stay on separate slips, one for access and one for restored flow.

dialogue.speaker: porter-idris
dialogue.text: A set of paper examples came in from the Nexus. I saved the tags with just one name. I’ve never needed more than one to take a crate to the right workshop. If there’s one name, one pair of hands did the work. Why would they leave anybody out? See the slip that says “Biro pen”?

options.text: Keep his example and look at one of the slips he passed over.
Leave the papers on Idris’s strap.

dialogue.speaker: porter-idris
dialogue.text: A short name helps me find a workshop on my rounds. I passed over the longer museum entry when I chose the examples for this strap. It’s in the sample tray on the way to the square.

dialogue.speaker: porter-idris
dialogue.text: Three jobs on one little pen. László József Bíró developed the design. His brother Georg helped with the ink. The Miles Martin Pen Company made this pen in Reading. Here’s the museum number, 1949-174/2. The patent office account is on the back. Which job would you guess from my tag?

options.text: Take that entry rather than another one-name tag.
Keep the entry in the sample tray.

dialogue.speaker: porter-idris
dialogue.text: The entry and the example tag refer to the same pen. You can take both to Idris. He has kept his other tag rather than dropping it when he heard you were coming.

dialogue.speaker: porter-idris
dialogue.text: I wrote “Biro” so I could find the bundle in a hurry. Now somebody wants to know where this pen was made. A short tag got my cart here. What should go on the strap for the next carrier?

options.text: Grant that a short mark can guide a delivery, then clip the named museum entry behind it.
Put the short tag and the museum entry side by side so the next carrier can check both.
Leave the papers at the strap for now.

dialogue.speaker: porter-idris
dialogue.text: I can still call out “Biro” from the cart. For the ink, lift this clip and look for Georg. I’ve left my thumb enough room to hold the page open.

dialogue.speaker: porter-idris
dialogue.text: Put the tags side by side. I could have sent a letter to the inventor asking about the Reading workshop. Now the next carrier can find the factory before the cart goes.

dialogue.speaker: porter-idris
dialogue.text: Two scouts brought me the same words this morning: turn blocked. One had the notes from the yard. The other carried a gate slip. The next carriers need to know what they can do with each report. Shall we change what the scouts carry, or arrange for someone to check the whole turn?

options.text: Put the turning notes in each scout’s hand first. Ask them to mark the opened gate and their instructions.
Keep the gate slips. Send a cart on a clear report and ask the lane keeper for a second look after a blocked one.
Leave both reports on the board for now.

dialogue.speaker: porter-idris
dialogue.text: I’ll copy the notes for the next shift. A marked report gives my carriers a place to try when two gates are still shut. They still have to look for room to turn on the lane itself.

dialogue.speaker: porter-idris
dialogue.text: The gate volunteers can still go ahead. I’ll leave a bell by the yard for blocked slips so the lane keeper can walk the turn. Tell a carrier to wait with a heavy cart until the keeper comes back.

dialogue.speaker: kip-arden
dialogue.text: One kettle. Two slips that say twelve. Hesper wants the yard open again. Sefa wants this slate out of the queue. I have three questions. I am going to finish the first one before I start on the other two.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: I can open before supper. I put a number on each repair and cross it off when it goes. The numbers worked on my bench. Ask the people standing outside with work to go home to if they want another closed gate.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: Once, we put the fee waivers on the same slate. Three people stopped coming. A black mark in the queue is a story the whole square can tell about you. They let me tell you about the wait. I promised to keep their names.

options.text: Take a copy of the collection rules and ask each of them to show you what happened.
Leave the slate for now.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: The two slips that say twelve came from different shifts. Put the rain-darkened pieces against the tag on this kettle. My trial was all from one shift.

options.text: Lay both twelves against the kettle tag and feel where the edges part.
Set the test pieces down.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: This plain edge slips past the little nick. This one meets it. Same figure, different fit. I can teach the apprentices to share a matching pair. I will have to stay by the hatch for their first shift.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: Here is a slip the owners let me show. One person had to say why they needed a waiver while the queue was listening. Another gave up a place in the queue and left the kettle. I wrote the times on a fresh copy. The names stayed on their page.

options.text: Fold the permitted copy beside the handoff rule. Keep the times on the outside.
Leave the copy folded for now.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: The times can go to Hana. That is the permission I was given. If the forge wants to keep a copy, the same rule holds there.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: The nick matched on the bench. Sefa has a slip she can share. Two marks buys us enough fresh blanks to make pairs for this shift. I can cut them now. The blanks cost the same if we end up keeping the gate shut.

options.text: Pay two marks for blank pairs.
Keep your marks. Return to the queue slate to choose what to do.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: Here are the paired pieces. When you go to the slate, you can open the yard with these, or keep the old gate shut and use the relay.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: Twelve knocked twice. The edge matched both the customer’s half and the tag on the kettle. See the space on the board for who checked the handoff? Sefa has my word that the fee slate stays inside.

options.text: Clip the checked half beside the finished kettle. Mark the pickup complete.
Leave the tag clipped to the kettle for now.

dialogue.speaker: kip-arden
dialogue.text: The kettle went to the right person. The queue has a mark it can check. We reached the end of a question! I am going to wait a whole minute before I ask the next one.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: Here is the kettle under a cloth. Hana can see the pickup slot on the outside of the tray. The fee slate stays here with me.

options.text: Lift the covered tray. Walk it to Hana’s return-slip stand west of the fountain.
Leave the tray on the shelf for now.

dialogue.speaker: stallkeeper-hana
dialogue.text: The repair has the same slot as the slip Sefa left me. Leave the tray under my counter. Take the spare stub back to the forge so they can see where it went.

options.text: Set the tray below the counter and take the return stub.
Keep hold of the tray for now.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: A return stub. That tells me where the kettle is. The owner can collect from Hana next round. Put the stub here and I can leave the hatch shut.

options.text: Clip the return stub to the slate and confirm the kettle’s pickup place.
Hold on to the stub for now.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: We kept a place for the kettle and left the fee inside. I will see if Hana can carry a tray after market tomorrow. That extra walk belongs to someone every time.

dialogue.speaker: kip-arden
dialogue.text: The apprentices took the slate back. It gives the next two pickup times now. A person who can come tomorrow will still find a way to the kettle. Anyone who missed the window has to ask for another one.

options.text: Read which shifts take appointments and pin the next hours where people can find them.
Leave the apprenticeship board alone.

dialogue.speaker: kip-arden
dialogue.text: The apprentices wrote down when to ask again. I can stop asking for them and come back when they have had a go.

dialogue.speaker: fruit-seller
dialogue.text: See the round edge? That is the return tray. I can pass it to you from this lane. Here at my stall, we also say “mek” to ask me for that tray when my eyes are on the scale.

options.text: Point to the return tray from the front lane.
Leave the return tray on its edge.

dialogue.speaker: fruit-seller
dialogue.text: The round one. I see your hand from here. I’ll set it within reach for the next pickup. Try from the path behind my stall while I keep looking over the front.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The same round edge is in sight. From the rear path you see Mara’s shoulder. Her eyes are still on the fruit and scale in front.

options.text: Point to the same tray while Mara faces the lane.
Say “mek” once and wait for a reply.
Step away from the stall.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Your hand is above the tray. Mara keeps setting fruit on her scale. You can still try the call she taught you from this spot.

options.text: Say “mek” once and wait for a reply.
Give the stall some room.

dialogue.speaker: fruit-seller
dialogue.text: I heard you that time. Here’s the tray. I have an extra round tab and a cord by the corner post. We can set which side should take the next pickup.

dialogue.speaker: fruit-seller
dialogue.text: The front faces me, so a low round tab lets a guest point at the right tray. The rear path stays free of the fruit queue. I can answer our pickup call from there while I’m on shift. Where should we set this tray?

options.text: Loop a round tab low on the front and set the tray below it.
Move the tray to the rear peg and ask Mara to answer the call.
Leave the tab and cord by the post.

dialogue.speaker: fruit-seller
dialogue.text: The round tab now sits just above the tray. Walk up from the front lane and try it where a guest would stand.

dialogue.speaker: fruit-seller
dialogue.text: I’ve set the tray on the rear peg. Go back around the stall and give our call one more try while my hands are on the scale.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The low round tab is in the lane’s clear view. Mara turns toward your hand as she brings her scale down.

options.text: Point to the round tab and take the tray when Mara offers it.
Let the next guest go first.

dialogue.speaker: fruit-seller
dialogue.text: You showed me which tray with your hand alone. I’ll leave this marker where everyone in the lane can see it. Keep the spare tab. It can mark a different pickup at a different stall.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The rear path has room for you. Mara is looking down at the fruit again. The tray is on the peg beside you.

options.text: Say “mek” here and take the tray when Mara taps it.
Leave the tray on the peg for the next pickup.

dialogue.speaker: fruit-seller
dialogue.text: I heard you before I saw you. The word works on this shift while I’m here to answer. Keep the spare round tab. Another stall could show the spot to someone who comes by with a different word.

missions.title: Two Tags on the Line
missions.knowledgeQuestion: When does a word name different checks for people doing different work?

objectives.title: Take the cuttings and the two “ready” slips.
Carry the same two cuttings into shade and open light.
Pin both checks at the end of the line.

missions.title: The Two-Bell Order
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What do two marks establish when people use them for different purposes?

objectives.title: Bring the guild stub and ferry strip for Order 34 together.
Line up the two records at the south-lane board.
Put the pair or the key by the buyer’s box.

missions.title: A Dry Step for the Washhouse
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What changes when we check a repair from where each person needs it to work?

objectives.title: Keep the intake reading and trace the water past the screen and tray.
Put a repair order on the washhouse board.
Check the change and leave a note for the next crew.

missions.title: The Mark and the Hands
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What is still useful in a reason after one of its claims has failed?

objectives.title: Bring the museum entry Idris left in the sample tray.
Return the entry and decide how the next carrier will see both pieces.

missions.title: The Scout’s Second Road
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What does a report let us infer when we know how it was made?

objectives.title: Set up the cart with each scout’s instructions and compare the two ledgers.
Leave an instruction for the scouts and carriers with Idris.

missions.title: The Repair Queue
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What does a person need to know to check a handoff, and who needs access to the rest?

objectives.title: Decide how the forge should handle the next pickup.
Follow the pickup route and check what the next person sees.

missions.title: A Tray at Either Side
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What changes when the same request reaches someone from a different place?

objectives.title: Try the same tray request from both sides of Mara’s stall.
Set up one side of the stall and collect the tray from there.

moments.did: You kept the cloth comparison and the ferry crew’s check in the same place so both groups could use the line.
moments.prompt: Who else might put “ready” to work in a different way?

moments.did: You kept the crew’s own marks beside the guild deadline and checked what each record could tell the buyer.
moments.prompt: Where else might two people shop or work by different ways of counting?

moments.did: You checked what changed for the washers and the carriers before making a claim about the repair.
moments.prompt: Where would you stand if you needed to check a different part of the job?

moments.did: You looked for the paper Idris had passed over and helped him keep the part of his first reason that worked.
moments.prompt: Which other paper would have changed the first story?

moments.did: You tried a point and a stall call from two sides of the counter, then helped Mara put the pickup where it could work.
moments.prompt: Who could use your setup without knowing the stall call?

journal.text: Two corners looked different on different hooks. They looked alike when we gave both the same light. I put that comparison where it could be checked, and left a separate tag for the folds the ferry crew needed to test.
The two parts of Order 34 fit. The deadline was in square bells. The marks on the ferry strip came from the two sides of a handover. No arrival time was recorded for this box.
The head reading showed water entering. The tail reading and the side run showed where it went. A workable walk and a working tray need separate checks.
The short tag could help a carrier find a door. The museum entry for this pen named two people. Idris changed the strap when he saw what his earlier choice of papers had left out.

A blocked report came from both kinds of scout. When the scout had the notes, switching would fit in four of the six setups. When the scout used only a slip, two setups showed the clear turn. Switching and holding fit just as often in the four blocked cases. Idris now has a way to tell his carriers what they need to check on the lane itself.
Two slips bore the same number. The pickup board can say where a repair went or when to come back without saying who needed time to pay.

hints.text: Two people may use the same word because each knows their own job.
The dyer checks how the colour looks. The ferry crew checks the folds before packing.
Use the cuttings near the south path and take both on one board.
Clip the two slips before walking west to the stands. The board carries both cuttings so you can compare them together.
One difference in the set-up might explain what looked like two colours.
Compare both cuttings under the same light, then change the light for both.
Use the shaded stand near the west tree and the open stand farther along the south lane.
Slide both cuttings into the shade. Then put the same board in the open light, or do the two in reverse. Keep each cutting fixed to the board.
The crew who packs the cloth needs a different check from the person comparing colour.
Give each check its own slip. Let the first reader see the one they can use.
Use the loose tags beside the southwest drying line after both comparisons.
Hang either the shared-light note or the folding check in front. Keep the other slip beside it.
Look for a record that names what the buyer ordered.
The guild spoke about the second bell. The crew may have meant a different thing.
Read the stub near the guild desk and the marked strip on the south side.
Clip both pieces marked Order 34. Their matching notches will let you line up the claims.
A mark and its context can travel separately.
Place the records beside each other before using either to tell the time.
Use the comparison board at the south lane after keeping both strips.
Line up the two Order 34 notches. Look for the empty arrival line after the two pieces meet.
The next reader should be able to tell the world what actually happened.
The buyer can use the two records under one heading. The crew can use a key for the markings already on the strip.
Visit the buyer’s box beside the comparison board to prepare the public copy.
Post either the separate headings on Order 34 or the key with a blank for a later order’s arrival. Both leave the old arrival time open.
Water on a step and a dry tray can belong to the same observation.
Follow the water after the head peg. Look at what enters the tray and what runs beside it.
The head peg is near the south path. The tail peg is beside the tray. The screen is farther west.
Clip all three readings in this round. Leave the intake in place so you can compare what reached each marker.
The other people using this lane may have a different repair in mind.
Clearing the screen tests flow. Marking a dry crossing helps people move now.
Use Hana’s small order board near the west well after checking the tray and screen.
Choose to clear the leaf mat or open the side step. Both routes still need a check.
The note should say what changed for this shift.
Check the same marks after the clearing, or see where the new step takes the carriers and what still reaches the tray.
Read the head peg near the south path a second time. Then check the tray after clearing or use the marked side step.
Leave the recheck note at your chosen site. Keep any job that still needs doing on the board.
Think about what a short name can help a carrier do.
Idris kept the short tag. Look for the museum entry behind it.
The sample tray is up the path from his strap, before the lantern stalls.
Take the museum entry with the object number. It refers to the same pen as the short tag.
Idris can keep the useful part of what he knew.
One clip could carry the longer entry behind the tag. You could also make it easy to compare both.
Return to Idris’s strap at the south path.
Clip the museum entry behind the tag or put the two side by side. Read what the next carrier will see.
The same chalk mark can lead to two different reports on the practice board.
Try the scout with turning notes. Then send a scout with just a slip.
Look for the practice cart board on the south edge of the market, east of the stone path.
Finish a cart run under each scout’s instructions. Open all six setups for both scouts and compare the blocked reports.
A carrier can hear the same report from a person following a different rule.
Decide who should know the turning notes and who should check a blocked turn before a loaded cart takes it.
Read the small board beside the practice cart after comparing both sets of setups.
Arrange for scouts to carry the turning notes or leave the slips in use with a second look after blocked reports.
Both people near the slate are trying to help someone collect a repair.
Check what Hesper’s number matches and what Sefa has permission to share.
Try Hesper’s two slips by the workbench and visit Sefa’s permission slip by the south stalls. Return to the west shelf when you are ready.
Pay two marks for pairs after both checks to open the side gate, use the covered tray after checking permission, or actively return the old slate to keep appointments.
See what a person can check today after your decision.
The yard verifies a pair. The relay uses a return stub. The appointments are on the outside slate.
The open side gate is west of the shelf. Hana’s relay stand is west of the fountain. The rota is where the old slate rested.
Clip the finished tag inside the open yard, carry the covered tray to Hana and return the stub to the shelf, or pin the next pickup windows from the outside board.
Mara has a round return tray at the Emberford fruit stall.
Start in front of Mara, where she can see your hand.
Walk behind the stall and try the same point with Mara facing away.
Stay on that side and try the agreed pickup call after the missed point.
Mara has a spare tab and a cord at the corner post.
The front has a clear view. The empty rear path suits a call Mara can hear.
Set the tray at the low tab in front or at the rear peg for Mara’s shift.
Try that same place from the guest’s lane and take the tray once Mara answers.

items.name: Mara’s round tray tab
items.description: The spare marker from Emberford’s tray. A clear position helped a visitor use it. Lantern Square has a marker rail at the repair counter.
